passage:
Friday

Sports day. I was SURE I'd win the 100 metres. I told everyone in the bus. I told Keerthana I'd beat her by ten steps. I even practised my winning pose in the mirror.

Then the whistle went and my legs felt like jelly. Keerthana was ahead from the start. I came fourth. FOURTH.

I just stood at the finish line with my mouth open. I didn't understand. In my head I was already on the podium.

Maa hugged me and said, "My brave boy, you ran well." But I didn't run well. I didn't even practise running. I only practised the pose.

Next year I'm going to practise the running part.

— Bhupen

qa.q: What position did Bhupen come in the race?
qa.a: Fourth.

qa.q: Why was Bhupen so stunned at the finish line?
qa.a: He had felt completely sure he would win, even practising a winning pose, so losing shocked and embarrassed him because his confidence was bigger than his preparation.

qa.q: What could Bhupen do before next year's race?
qa.a: Practise actual running a few times a week and see his real times, so his confidence matches his speed.

qa.q: How might Keerthana have felt when Bhupen boasted about winning by ten steps?
qa.a: Keerthana may have felt annoyed or challenged, and then quietly pleased when she won.

grounding: It shows a boy who is certain he will win a race and is stunned when he loses, his confidence louder than his preparation.

passage: At the quiz competition in the village school near Karnal, Chetan's hand shot up before the teacher finished the question. "Which is the largest planet?" "Saturn!" he shouted, grinning at his friend Imran. Saturn had the big rings; it had to be the biggest. He was so sure that he didn't even hear the teacher say, "Anyone else?" Imran said quietly, "Jupiter." The teacher smiled. "Correct." Chetan's mouth fell open. He stared at the chart on the wall. There it was: Jupiter, bigger than everything. He felt his ears go hot. He had been so certain. He sat down and didn't raise his hand for the next three questions, even when he knew the answer.

qa.q: What did Chetan answer for the largest planet?
qa.a: Saturn.

qa.q: Why did Chetan feel so sure Saturn was the answer?
qa.a: Saturn's big rings made it seem the biggest, and his quick, loud confidence felt like knowledge, so being wrong left him stunned and embarrassed.

qa.q: What could Chetan try in the next quiz?
qa.a: He could pause for a second to check how he knows the answer before shouting, and still try again after being wrong.

qa.q: How might Imran have felt when he answered correctly?
qa.a: Imran may have felt quietly proud, and maybe a little awkward correcting his friend.

grounding: It shows a boy who is certain of a quiz answer and is stunned when wrong, his confidence louder than his knowledge.

passage: At the public pool in Mexico City, Javier told his cousin Diego, "I'll beat you to the other end. Easy." He'd been swimming for one summer; Diego had been in a club for three years. Javier didn't think that mattered. He felt fast. He was fast, in his head. The lifeguard blew the whistle. Javier splashed wildly for ten metres, then swallowed water and had to grab the rope. Diego was already touching the far wall. Javier hung on the rope, coughing, completely stunned. "How?" he gasped. Diego swam back, grinning. "You were really sure, eh?" Javier's face burned. He had been so, so sure. That evening he asked Diego to show him how to breathe properly.

qa.q: What did Javier grab after swallowing water?
qa.a: The rope.

qa.q: Why did Javier feel so sure he would win?
qa.a: He felt fast in his head and didn't count Diego's three years of club training, so his confidence felt like proof until he was stunned and embarrassed.

qa.q: What step did Javier take after losing, and why is it wise?
qa.a: He asked Diego to teach him proper breathing, learning the real skill instead of relying on feeling fast.

qa.q: How does Diego seem to see Javier's challenge?
qa.a: Diego seems amused and friendly, teasing a little but happy to help later.

grounding: It shows a boy who is certain he can win a race and is stunned when wrong, his confidence louder than his skill.

passage: In the school library during the free period, Baljeet flipped through the history textbook. "Easy. I know all this." Every page looked familiar; he'd read it in class. His classmate Preeti was making flashcards. "You're not revising?" "No need. I've seen it all." Preeti held up a card. "When was the Battle of Plassey, and who fought it?" Baljeet opened his mouth. He knew the page. He could picture the map. But the year wouldn't come. "It's... the one with the East India Company." "Year?" "Seventeen... something." Preeti raised an eyebrow. "And the other side?" Silence. Baljeet laughed, a bit awkwardly. "I'll know it in the exam." Preeti shrugged and went back to her cards. He looked at the textbook again. It still looked easy. That was the problem.

qa.a: Flashcards.

qa.q: Why did the history syllabus feel easy to Baljeet?
qa.a: Every page looked familiar, so he felt confident and sure he knew it, mistaking recognising the material for being able to recall it.

qa.q: What could Baljeet do to test how well he really knows the chapter?
qa.a: He could close the book and try answering questions from memory, like Preeti's flashcards, before deciding he's ready.

passage: In Buenos Aires, Valentina was sure her band's first real gig would sell out. She booked the big hall downtown, not the small bar where they usually played. She paid the deposit from the money she'd saved for a trip. Felix, the drummer, said, "Maybe start smaller?" She laughed. "People love us. It'll be packed." She didn't plan what would happen if it wasn't. On the night, forty people came to a room built for four hundred. The echo made their songs sound thin. Valentina smiled on stage, but afterwards she sat in the empty hall, shaking. It wasn't only the money. She had been so certain that she'd never let herself imagine this. Felix sat beside her. "It's one night." "I know," she said. "It just feels like everything."

qa.q: How many people came to the gig?
qa.a: Forty people.

qa.q: Why did the empty hall hurt Valentina so much?
qa.a: She had been so certain of success that she never imagined failure, so the empty room felt crushing and she was left shaking.

qa.q: What could Valentina have done to leave a margin for error?
qa.a: She could have started with a smaller venue, as Felix suggested, or planned what to do if fewer people came.

qa.q: How does Felix seem to respond to Valentina's disappointment?

grounding: It shows a young adult so certain her plan would work that she left no margin for error, making the failure hurt more.

passage: In the hospital's IT department in Shillong, Sunaina said in the Monday meeting, "The new billing system will be ready by Friday. Hundred percent." She sounded completely sure. Pema, the team lead, felt a flicker of worry. The last two times, Sunaina's "hundred percent" had turned into two extra weeks. But Pema didn't want to crush her either; Sunaina was talented. After the meeting, Pema asked her quietly, "What's the earliest it could be ready, and what's the latest if things go wrong?" Sunaina paused. "Earliest, Friday. If testing finds bugs... maybe the Wednesday after." "And the worst case?" "If the old data doesn't transfer... two weeks." Pema nodded. "Thanks. I'll tell the finance team the Wednesday after, and we'll celebrate if it's Friday." Sunaina looked relieved.

qa.q: When did Sunaina say the billing system would be ready?
qa.a: By Friday.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling when Sunaina said 'hundred percent'?
qa.a: Pema felt a flicker of worry, remembering past delays, but also didn't want to crush a talented colleague.

qa.q: Why was asking for a range and worst case wise?
qa.a: It turned certainty into a realistic plan, so Pema could tell finance a safer date without punishing or blindly trusting Sunaina.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel after the conversation?
qa.a: Sunaina seemed relieved, perhaps glad to share her real doubts without being judged.

grounding: It shows a team lead who hears a colleague promise fast delivery with total certainty and wisely asks for a range and worst case.

passage:
Hi Karthik,

Thanks for saying in today's call that the app update will be live by Tuesday. I really appreciate your energy, and you've pulled off hard things before.

Since the client is planning their launch around our date, could you help me with something? Instead of one date, could you give me three:
- the earliest it could realistically be done,
- the most likely date,
- the latest if something goes wrong (for example, if the payment module needs changes).

I'm not doubting you. I just want to give the client a date we can keep, and plan for backup if needed.

Let's talk tomorrow at ten?

Thanks,
Baljeet

qa.a: Baljeet seems appreciative of Karthik's energy but a bit cautious, wanting to protect the client launch from an over-sure date.

qa.q: Why does asking for three dates help the team?
qa.a: It replaces a single confident promise with a realistic range, so the team can plan for delays without blaming or blindly trusting Karthik.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel reading this email?
qa.a: Karthik may feel respected rather than doubted, and perhaps a little relieved to share the risks.

grounding: It shows a lead who responds to a colleague's certain promise by asking for a range and worst case instead of punishing or blindly trusting it.

passage: In the agriculture office at Hingoli, Yamini had a small notebook that her colleague Reena teased her about. At the start of every season, Yamini wrote predictions: "Soybean yield in Kalamnuri block will be above average: 80% sure." "Rain will come by mid-June: 70% sure." After harvest, she checked each one and marked a tick or a cross. After two years, she sat down and counted. Her yield guesses at eighty percent were right almost every time. But her rain guesses at seventy percent were right only half the time. She felt a bit humbled. "So I'm good at reading fields, not skies," she told Reena. Now, when she advised farmers about sowing dates, she said, "I'm not very sure about rain, so let's also check the weather office." The farmers trusted her more for it.

qa.q: How often were Yamini's seventy-percent rain guesses right?

qa.a: She now tells farmers when she's unsure about rain and checks the weather office, relying on her strength in reading fields.

qa.q: How might the farmers see Yamini's honesty?
qa.a: The farmers trusted her more, valuing that she admits where she's unsure.

grounding: It shows a grounded professional who writes predictions with percentages, checks them later, and learns where her sure feelings are reliable.

Remember I told you last month I'd mastered marketing after learning the SWOT analysis? I was going around analysing everything: the canteen, my cousin's bakery, even our hostel football team.

Well. This week our professor gave us a real case: a tea company losing customers in three states, with conflicting data and a new competitor. My SWOT looked like a child's drawing next to what the case needed. Pricing, distribution, customer surveys. I didn't know half the terms.

Tushar

grounding: It shows a student whose confidence peaked after a simple course, then dropped on harder problems before real skill grew.

passage: It was the week before the product launch, and the office in Aizawl was in chaos: the server kept crashing, and the lead engineer was sick. Lalremsiami, only two years into her job, quietly fixed the crash in an afternoon. She thought it was nothing. "Anyone could do it. It was just a memory leak." Mahima, the project manager, stared. "Three people tried for two days." Lalremsiami shrugged. "They were busy." When Mahima asked her to present the fix to the team, she panicked. "I'm not senior enough. What if they ask something I don't know?" That night she read three articles about memory leaks, sure she'd missed something obvious. She hadn't. But the more she knew, the more she saw what she didn't, and the smaller she felt.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami fix in an afternoon?
qa.a: The server crash.

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami think anyone could have fixed the crash?
qa.a: What was easy for her felt easy for everyone, so she doubted her own skill and felt anxious about presenting.

qa.q: How could Mahima help Lalremsiami see her real ability?
qa.a: Mahima could point out specifically that three people tried for two days, and encourage her to present with support.

qa.q: How does Mahima see Lalremsiami's fix?
qa.a: Mahima is surprised and impressed, knowing others failed for two days.

grounding: It shows a skilled young engineer who assumes what's easy for her is easy for everyone and doubts her ability despite real skill.

passage: Rehana had been at the Hyderabad engineering firm for three years, and she was the one everyone came to when the design software broke. She fixed it in minutes, usually while eating lunch. But when the promotion to senior engineer opened up, she didn't apply. "Charu should do it," she told her friend. "She's much better than me." Charu, who sat next to her, had asked Rehana for help four times that week. At home, Rehana made a list of everything she didn't know: new software versions, advanced load calculations, three certifications. The list was long. It made her feel small. She didn't make a list of what she did know. When Charu found out, she laughed. "Rehana, I ask you for help every day. Who do you think is better?" Rehana didn't have an answer.

qa.q: How many times had Charu asked Rehana for help that week?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: Why didn't Rehana apply for the promotion?
qa.a: She felt doubtful and small, focusing on what she didn't know, and assumed that what was easy for her was easy for others.

qa.q: What could Rehana do to see her skill more fairly?
qa.a: She could also list what she does know and how often others ask her for help, then consider applying.

qa.q: How does Charu see Rehana's ability?
qa.a: Charu sees Rehana as clearly more skilled, since she relies on her help every day.

grounding: It shows a skilled young engineer who doubts her ability and assumes her skills are common, seeing only her gaps.

passage:
"Kashish, the client loved your bridge calculations."
"Really, Sudha? It was just standard stuff."
"Standard? They'd rejected two other firms because of those calculations."
"I just followed the codes. Anyone could do that."
"Anyone did not do that. Anyone got it wrong."
"Maybe they were rushed."
"You always say that. Why don't you believe you're good?"
"Because every time I learn something, I see ten more things I don't know. The better I get, the more I see what's missing."
"That's what makes you good."
"It doesn't feel like that. It feels like I'm always behind."
Sudha shook her head. "You're the only one on the team who worries about that. The rest of us just wing it."
Kashish laughed, but she still didn't look convinced.

qa.q: How many other firms had the client rejected?
qa.a: Two other firms.

qa.q: Why does Kashish feel she's always behind despite her skill?
qa.a: The more Kashish learns, the more gaps she sees, so she feels doubtful and assumes what's easy for her is standard.

qa.q: What could help Kashish see her work fairly?
qa.a: She could keep a record of specific wins, like the client's praise, alongside what she's still learning.

qa.q: How does Sudha see Kashish's self-doubt?
qa.a: Sudha finds it frustrating and a little funny, seeing Kashish as clearly skilled.

grounding: It shows a skilled young engineer who assumes what's easy for her is easy for everyone and doubts her ability as awareness of gaps grows.

passage: Binita, you're mentoring your first newcomer? Let me tell you about Rohan, when I was a young team lead in Kolkata. Rohan joined us sure he knew everything about databases. In his first week, he told a client our system was badly designed. My colleague wanted to shout at him in front of everyone. I didn't. I sat with him and asked, "Walk me through how you'd back up this database, step by step." He started confidently. By step three, he stopped. He didn't know how to handle the live data. I didn't say anything. He went quiet, then said, "I think I need to learn this part." I gave him two specific examples from past projects. He studied them for a week. Later he became our best database engineer. So, Binita, don't mock. Ask them to explain, step by step. That's Arnab's way.

qa.q: What did Arnab ask Rohan to walk through?
qa.a: How he'd back up the database, step by step.

qa.q: How did young Arnab feel when his colleague wanted to shout at Rohan?
qa.a: Arnab felt that shouting would only make Rohan defensive, and chose calm patience instead.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped Rohan see his gaps?
qa.a: Arnab asked him to explain the task step by step and gave specific examples, letting Rohan find the gaps himself.

qa.q: How might Rohan have felt when he stopped at step three?
qa.a: Rohan probably felt surprised and humbled, realising for himself what he didn't know.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how Arnab asked an overconfident newcomer to explain a task step by step so the gaps showed for themselves.

passage: The project deadline was in two days and the Chennai office was short-staffed, so Zeenat had no time for long training. Her new team member, Vandana, had announced on day one, "Report automation? I've done it before, it's simple." When the first report came out full of wrong totals, a senior engineer muttered, "Useless," loud enough to hear. Vandana's face went red, and she insisted the data was wrong, not her code. Zeenat took her aside. "Show me how your code works, step by step." Vandana began confidently, then stopped at the part where the totals were calculated. "Oh. I'm adding them twice." Zeenat nodded. "That's okay. Here's an example from last month's report that handles it." Vandana fixed it in an hour. Later she said, "The shouting made me defensive. The walk-through made me see."

qa.q: What did the senior engineer mutter?
qa.a: "Useless."

qa.q: How did Vandana feel after the senior engineer's comment?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and defensive, her face red, insisting the data was wrong instead of her code.

qa.q: Why did Zeenat's step-by-step approach work better than ridicule?
qa.a: Asking Vandana to explain her code let her find the error herself, while the ridicule only made her defend her false confidence.

qa.q: How might the senior engineer see Zeenat's approach?
qa.a: The senior engineer might be surprised that patience worked faster than criticism.

grounding: It shows a mentor who asks a newcomer to explain a task step by step with specific examples, while blunt ridicule only hardens false confidence.

passage: In the Mumbai marketing agency, Keerthana joined the team announcing she could handle any social media campaign. "I've grown my own page to five thousand followers." Nikita, her mentor, noticed that Keerthana's first campaign plan had no budget, no target audience and no way to measure results. Some colleagues rolled their eyes. One said, "Five thousand followers, wow, a real expert." Keerthana heard it and became more defensive. Nikita invited her for chai. "Walk me through the plan, step by step. Who is the customer? How will we know it worked?" Keerthana began, then paused. "I... didn't think about measuring." Nikita showed her two old campaign reports. "See how these track results each week?" Keerthana read them quietly. The next day she brought a new plan, with numbers. "Thanks for not laughing," she said.

qa.q: How many followers had Keerthana grown her own page to?
qa.a: Five thousand followers.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel when she heard the sarcastic comment?
qa.a: She felt stung and became more defensive, holding tighter to her confidence.

qa.q: What made Nikita's approach effective?
qa.a: Asking Keerthana to explain step by step and showing specific examples helped her discover the gaps without shame.

qa.q: How might the colleague who mocked Keerthana feel seeing her new plan?
qa.a: The colleague may feel surprised, and perhaps a little embarrassed about the sarcasm.

grounding: It shows a mentor who helps an overconfident newcomer see gaps through step-by-step explanation and examples, while ridicule only makes her defensive.

passage: The power went out in the second half of the cricket final, so Farhan, ten, and his sister Ankita listened to the last overs on their neighbour's radio, huddled in the dark. Before the match, Farhan had said, "Mumbai will win easily." At the halfway point, he said, "Hmm, could go either way." With five overs left, he chewed his nails and said, "I really don't know." Then Chennai won by two wickets. Farhan jumped up. "I knew it! I knew Chennai would win all along!" Ankita stared at him. "You said Mumbai would win easily." "No I didn't. I said Chennai's bowling was better." "You never said that." "I was thinking it." Farhan crossed his arms, completely sure. In his head, he really had known.

qa.q: Who did Farhan say would win before the match?
qa.a: Mumbai would win easily.

qa.q: Why does Farhan feel sure he knew Chennai would win?
qa.a: After the match, his mind quietly rewrote his earlier uncertainty into a neat story, so he genuinely feels proud and certain he knew.

qa.q: What could help Farhan notice this next time?
qa.a: He could write his prediction on paper before the match and check it afterward.

qa.q: How does Ankita see Farhan's claim?
qa.a: Ankita finds it confusing and a bit annoying, since she clearly remembers him saying Mumbai.

grounding: It shows a boy who, after a match ends, says he knew the result all along, rewriting his earlier uncertainty.

passage: In their Delhi flat, Kamal and his mother Anjali watched the school football final from the stands on Saturday. Before the game, Kamal said, "Green House is stronger. Red House will lose." During the game, Red House scored first, and Kamal said, "Maybe Red House is better." At half-time it was one-all, and he admitted, "I have no idea who'll win." In the last minute, Green House scored. They won two-one. Kamal clapped wildly. "I told you! I knew from the start Green House would win!" His mother smiled. "At half-time you said you had no idea." "I was just saying that," Kamal said. "I always knew." On the way home, he told his father on the phone, "I predicted it exactly." Anjali said nothing, but she smiled out of the auto window.

qa.q: What was the final score?
qa.a: Two-one to Green House.

qa.q: Why does Kamal feel he 'always knew' Green House would win?
qa.a: After the win, his mind rewrote the uncertain middle of the game, so he genuinely felt proud and sure he had predicted it.

qa.q: What could Anjali do to help Kamal notice his changing guesses?
qa.a: She could ask him to write down his guess before the next game, and then look at it together after.

qa.q: How does Anjali seem to see Kamal's claim?
qa.a: Anjali seems amused and fond, noticing the rewrite but not arguing.

grounding: It shows a boy who, after a match ends, claims he knew the result all along, as his mind rewrites earlier uncertainty.
